title: Africa’s green industrial future: regional demand as the missing puzzle
body:
We talk a lot about skills, finance, and technology in Africa’s green industrialization.

But green industrialization doesn’t move on abstractions. It moves when demand is organized at scale.

Amid Africa's fragmented market, this is why regional demand is not a nice-to-have—it is the lifeline of Africa’s green industrial future.

So what does regional demand actually look like in practice?

- Fertilizer corridors, where multiple countries commit to long-term offtake of green ammonia and green urea—giving firms the confidence to invest in local production and skills.
- Green steel for African infrastructure, where roads, rail, ports, and housing projects pool procurement across borders—turning construction pipelines into industrial anchors.
- Electric mobility for public transport, where cities aggregate orders for electric buses and fleets—supporting regional assembly, maintenance, and charging ecosystems.
- Regional battery value chains, where standardized specifications and pooled procurement create markets for battery assembly, recycling, and systems integration.

This is what demand looks like when it is bankable, predictable, and continental.

The lesson is simple but often ignored: Regional demand is not theoretical. It is planned, coordinated, and procured.

This is where the AfCFTA becomes decisive—not as a trade agreement, but as a demand-aggregating industrial instrument.

When demand is organized at scale, firms invest.

When firms invest, technology transfer occurs and skills emerge. Ultimately, markets, skills, and production grow together.

When this happens, green industrialization becomes real.

The real question is no longer whether Africa has the resources or the talent. It is whether Africa is willing to organize demand at scale.

This is the true test of Africa’s green industrialization.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon OwusuEmmanuel Buadi Mensah Woubet Kassa, PhD Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Rex Asiama (PhD)
